title: Visit the graves
hook: the Prophet encouraged visiting graves, for they remind of death and the hereafter (Sahih Muslim)

segments.voice: Yesterday, a father at his dying son's side, and the line, this is mercy. Did you let anyone cry without hurrying them? Today, the same Prophet, standing at a grave. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

A grave, and a grown man standing at it, crying. It's his mother's grave, and he has come to see where she lies. The people who came with him start crying too, because he is. The man is the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the scene is in Sahih Muslim, a collection of reports of his words and deeds. When he speaks, he ends with advice for everyone standing there, and for anyone who has ever avoided a cemetery.
screen: `A MAN AT HIS MOTHER'S GRAVE.` → `EVERYONE AROUND HIM WEEPS.` → `THEN HE SPEAKS.`

segments.voice: First, a change of mind. In another report in Sahih Muslim, the Prophet says something surprising: I had forbidden you to visit graves, but now visit them. A rule was set, then lifted. The report keeps both halves, the old no and the new yes, in a single sentence. Second, the reason. At his mother's grave, he gives it plainly: visit the graves, for they remind you of death. In other collections the reports add that they remind you of the hereafter. Either way, the point isn't to stay sad. A grave is a teacher. It doesn't lecture. It just stands there, with a name on it, saying: this happens to everyone, and then comes what comes next. Third, a greeting. The hadith don't picture walking into a cemetery in silence. Reports in the same collection describe a greeting addressed to the people in the graves: peace be upon you, dwellers of these homes, believers; and we, God willing, will join you. The dead are spoken to as neighbors. Fourth, they remind us. It's easy to arrange a life that never passes a grave. In some towns, cemeteries sit at the edge, behind walls. This hadith turns that around: go on purpose, so the living remember they are on the same road. In Muslim teaching, the visit is both a kindness to the dead, with prayers for them, and a kindness to the living, a reminder while there's still time to use it. They remind us.
screen: `FORBIDDEN, THEN ENCOURAGED.` · `GRAVES REMIND YOU OF DEATH.` · `GREET THE DEAD AS NEIGHBORS.` · `GO ON PURPOSE.` · then, large: `THEY REMIND US.`

segments.voice: Sit and let the breath settle. Bring to mind a grave you know. A grandparent's, a friend's, or a stranger's you once walked past. See the ground, the stone, the name. If no grave comes to mind, think of a place where someone's ashes rest, or a memorial bench. Stand there in your mind for a while. Let it remind you of what it reminds you of, without pushing. If you pray, you can greet the dead there, or ask mercy for them, in words you already know. The bell holds the time.
Sahih Muslim, the hadith collection where the Prophet, having once forbidden it, now tells people to visit graves, because they remind the living of death. Today's word.
Your line: they remind us. This week, visit a grave or a cemetery if you can, even for five minutes, and let it remind you. Day seven hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Muslims visit graves, in some communities on Fridays or around the Eids, greeting the dead with a salam, reciting Quran and praying for mercy for them; practices such as praying to the dead or wailing at graves are discouraged.

notes: Sahih Muslim 976 paraphrased: the Prophet visits his mother's grave, weeps, those around him weep; 'visit the graves, for they remind you of death'. The hadith also says he asked permission to seek forgiveness for her and was not granted it; that detail is deliberately left out. Keeper: confirm the omission is fair.
Sahih Muslim 977 paraphrased ('I had forbidden you to visit graves, but now visit them'); confirm number.
The greeting (974–975) is paraphrased, not quoted; confirm wording.
'In other collections... remind you of the hereafter': Ibn Majah reference given as 1569; please confirm the number.
'One of the major collections' was cut; the hook now says 'a collection of reports of his words and deeds'.
'It's easy to arrange a life that never passes a grave' is a general observation; soften if needed.
howItsDone: Fridays and Eids are customary in some communities, not required; confirm.

Audit: the hook said his words at the grave were 'not about his mother's story', but in Sahih Muslim 976 he first speaks of her (asking permission for her); now 'he ends with advice for everyone'. 'Many towns' softened; carry no longer repeats day 781's read-a-name task.

Editor: cut 'one of the major collections' (superlative-like claim); 'Muslims don't walk into a cemetery in silence' reframed as what the hadith picture (and the myth to match); fixed the garbled 'a reminder before it's too late to need one'; removed narrator instructions ('not to wallow'); word line reordered for clarity; howItsDone 'often' softened.
